summary: Probable observation of atmospheric reentry
description: On November 12, 1984, at around 7:00 PM, several witnesses observed a white ball, about the size of a soccer ball, with a bright red tail approximately 2 meters long, above the coastline for a period of 5 to 6 seconds. The object moved slowly, silently, and at low altitude, following a straight trajectory. This phenomenon exhibited the characteristics of atmospheric reentry.

summary: Likely sighting of a disco projector
description: On October 25, 1994, at approximately 7:40 PM, a witness and his wife observed a white ball that was initially stationary and then regularly oscillated from right to left, changing color from pink to green. The phenomenon described was likely the observation of a laser advertising projector, commonly used by nightclubs.

summary: Beam of light from a helicopter headlight
description: On October 22, 1984, at approximately 6:50 p.m., two motorists spotted an intense light near a railway track. It was shaped like a white sphere, from which a sharp white beam emanated. Because the car windows were closed, no noise was heard. The investigation revealed that it was the 600-watt searchlight of a Puma helicopter on approach to land at the nearby military base.

summary: Spotlights
description: On October 2, 1984, between 11:30 PM and 11:42 PM, a witness and his wife noticed an unusual brightness through their window. This yellow light appeared to be coming from a straight line of spotlights. During the 12 minutes of observation, one beam became more distinct and illuminated the ground. A movement of the spotlights was noticed, but no sound was heard. This brightness faded until the light went out completely. No further information was gathered about this phenomenon.

summary: Observations of an orange glow in the shape of a rugby ball: Moon misinterpretation.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, classified at the time, which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even an explicit change in classification within an investigation report. This particular case is among those classified as D in 1984 by GEIPAN. On September 28, 1984, between 8:30 and 8:50 PM, five witnesses observed the slow movement of an orange glow in the sky, the size and shape of a rugby ball. During the observation, this glow split into two oval parts and evolved in a way that puzzled the witnesses. The described phenomenon shares many characteristics (duration of observation, shape, size, color) with a well-known astronomical object: the Moon at sunset. Furthermore, the Moon was clearly visible in the observed area of the sky, even though the witnesses did not mention it. The issue is not the witnesses' visual perception, but rather their interpretation of the observation based on their feelings (astonishment, fatigue, nighttime observation). In the current GEIPAN classification, this case of moderate strangeness is classified as UAP A, an observation linked to a misinterpretation of the Moon.

summary: Observations on several occasions during a vehicle journey of the presence of a red/orange Pan at low altitude: observations of the Moon.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, originally classified as A, B, C, or D, which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even an explicit change in classification within an investigation report. This observation, previously classified as D, is part of a group of cases recently re-examined. On September 3, 1984, around midnight, two, then three witnesses in a car were intrigued by the presence of a very bright red-orange phenomenon at low altitude. Witnesses spotted the UFO at several locations along their route between Les Fontanettes (Saint-Aubin-en-Bay), Le Coudray-Saint-Germer, and the Champignolle crossroads (Serifontaine). No sound emanating from this object was heard during the intermittent observations. Frightened, the witnesses turned back. One of the witnesses (T1) had already made a similar observation while driving with his mother (T4) in July 1984. This case is consistent (3 witnesses), and the description of the observation location and the observed UFO is precise (see the investigation notes). The described phenomenon shares many characteristics (duration of observation, shape, size, color, etc.) with a known astronomical phenomenon: the Moon at sunset. The length of the observation period (half an hour or three-quarters of an hour), as well as the fact that the UFO seemed to follow the motorists (a tracking sphere), suggests the observation of an astronomical phenomenon. The appearance described by the witnesses leaves no doubt: a large, luminous object, low on the southwest horizon, orange or red in color. A witness's specific description (e.g., "It was still round, but a piece was missing on the left, as if a crescent were missing") even suggests that the Moon was then in its gibbous phase, between the First Quarter and the Full Moon. The presence of the Moon in the observed direction is verified. The witnesses' descriptions are very precise thanks to the alignment with the road, and this corresponds perfectly. Similarly, the Moon was indeed in the expected gibbous phase. Finally, the witnesses make no mention of the Moon, even though it was clearly present in the different directions observed. Mistaken identity involving the Moon is a frequent occurrence in the records of GEIPAN (see case search on the website www.geipan.fr using the keyword "Moon"). What may be surprising here is the apparent absence of cloud cover or clouds that could have exacerbated the misinterpretation. The Moon is clearly described as round or nearly so; this is not one of those curious red shapes caused by breaks in the clouds in front of the Moon. It is worth noting that the witnesses are young, and this may be their first experience. However, this observation created a strong sense of unease and shock: at 1: I panicked, I was very scared; at 2: I told XXX, "Quick, let's turn back!"; at 3: I was really very scared, I had tears in my eyes (T1); at 4: I didn't stop, I think it was out of fear; at 5: the three of us wondered if we should continue; at 6: we fled to Le Coudray; at 7: all three of us were gripped by panic. XXX was crying in the car because she had been very scared (T2); at 8: we couldn't go any further; at 9: XXX was shouting in the car (T3). GEIPAN classifies the case as A: observation of the Moon.

summary: Very bright white light moving across the sky
description: On August 31, 1984, between 9:00 and 9:15 PM, two witnesses observed a large, stationary white light below the moon. During the following 10 minutes of observation, this light elongated, taking the shape of a rugby ball, moved above the moon, and separated into two distinct white lights. According to the witnesses, these lights appeared to be connected by a compact mass. No noise or smoke was observed. The phenomenon disappeared abruptly. No further information has been gathered about this event.

summary: object observed through binoculars.
description: On August 2, 1984, at 2:04 AM, a witness observed a cylindrical object for three seconds. The object was stationary at first, then began to move. Observation through binoculars revealed a yellow line along the axis of the cylinder, parallel to the direction of its movement. No further information about this phenomenon has been gathered.

summary: Probable star observations
description: Between July 29 and August 2, 1984, several witnesses observed bright, star-like objects in the sky. These objects emitted flashes of red and green light. The observations were made at night, after a hot day, under clear skies. Over the course of these nights of observation, the objects' positions varied considerably. The star chart shows that the observed region was the constellation Perseus, which at this time of year is the site of numerous luminous phenomena known as the Perseids. The witnesses likely observed this type of phenomenon.

summary: bright object in the sky
description: On April 27, 1984, several witnesses observed a very bright, triangular object above two towns in the Isère department: it remained stationary and could be seen for between fifteen minutes and one hour thirty-five minutes. Two witnesses saw the object rise and gradually disappear after a thick plume of smoke appeared. No other information was gathered about this phenomenon.

summary: Observations of the evolution of an elongated, very bright object moving rapidly and silently from right to left and from top to bottom in the cloudy sky: lack of information.
description: On Saturday, March 24, 1984, starting at 5:50 a.m., five nuns from a convent observed the movements of a UFO (Unidentified Flying Object) in the morning sky for ten minutes. This oval-shaped object shone brightly in the night sky, moving very rapidly from left to right and from bottom to top. The witnesses ceased their observation to resume their activities, leaving the UFO still visible to the east. This case (formerly known as SARAMON (32)) is part of a series of sightings currently being re-examined (see the Investigation Notes document). This case is consistent (five witnesses), and the description of the observed UFO is quite precise. The sincerity and credibility of the witnesses have never been questioned. The described phenomenon presents many common characteristics (duration of observation, shape, size, color) with a skytracer-type light animation. Furthermore, the date of the observation (Saturday morning) corresponds to a typical day for the use of this device, and there were clouds present that could reflect a skytracer. However, due to the unique nature of the observation by the same witnesses or neighbors, and the impossibility of verifying it with nightclubs of the time, this hypothesis could not be confirmed. It is not the visual perception of the witnesses that is in question, but The interpretation that these individuals make of their observation through their feelings (astonishment, nighttime observation of an artificial device that was new at the time). In the current GEIPAN classification, this case of weak strangeness is classified as C e, due to a lack of corroborating evidence, although it resembles a case of mistaken identity with a skytracer.

summary: Very long observations (2 hours) by two witnesses of a very bright circular phenomenon in the sky; disappearance at daybreak: observations of the planet Venus.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, classified at the time (A, B, C, or D), which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This observation, previously classified as D and named LA FOA (988) 05.03.1984, is part of a set of cases recently re-examined. This case concerns the observation of a UFO by several residents of the town of LA FOA (988) on different dates (the 2nd and 5th, and an unknown date) in March 1984 (see the investigation report). On March 7, 1984, the gendarmerie was notified that several people in a neighborhood of La Foa, New Caledonia, had repeatedly observed luminous phenomena in the sky. The gendarmerie investigation, recorded in a single report, states that: - on March 5, 1984, between 4:30 and 6:30 a.m., two witnesses in a car (T1 and T2) observed a particularly bright phenomenon in the sky for a very long time. - on March 2, 1984, around 8:00 p.m., two witnesses at home (T3 and T4) observed a fireball emitting a white light. - and on a date he does not recall, but still in March 1984, another witness (T5) observed a "broad band of light" on three separate occasions from his home. A final witness (T6) was interviewed by the police because he was mentioned in T5's statement. However, this last witness made no observations. The witnesses, or pairs of witnesses, observed a UFO at different dates and times, and the positions and movements of the UFOs were themselves different. It is necessary to seek an explanation specific to each of the three observations (T1-T2, T3-T4, and T5) without initially assuming that they might be the same phenomenon. Furthermore, the police intervened following a rumor about residents having repeatedly seen luminous shapes in the sky. No witness spontaneously reported their observation. Due to this rumor and the approximate cross-checking of witness accounts, it is possible that the strangeness reported by witnesses in their statements was stronger than that experienced at the time of the observation, and that, taken in isolation, some observations might have gone unnoticed. The preceding may explain the anecdotal or at least inconsistent nature of T5's report: - the witness no longer knows if it was the day before or two days before (e.g., One or two days ago e), which is never the case when the observation is truly strange; - the available information is imprecise (not only regarding the date) and does not allow for any precise analysis (e.g., "A wide band of light, illuminating the sky intensely, occurred on three different occasions. It looked like the passage of a very bright object moving from right to left above the trees facing my house e"); - the witness has an initial meteorological explanation, which does not eliminate the perceived strangeness but reduces its magnitude (e.g., "For a while, I thought it was a sign of bad weather, while still being shocked by this phenomenon." e); - In the current context, given the limited information available, we cannot rule out the possibility that a particular configuration of vehicle headlight beams projected into the sky could have produced an initial, limited sense of strangeness that was retrospectively amplified. The T5 observation is of very low consistency (both in terms of information and reliability) considering the available data 35 years later. This observation, which appears to have a rather low level of strangeness, is unusable (Class C) due to a lack of reliable information. Conversely, the accounts of T1 and T2 describe a real level of perceived strangeness (even if this may have increased after the observation) and provide a good level of information. These two witnesses undoubtedly mistook Venus for another object. - The described appearance of the UFO is consistent: a luminous sphere, white color, and high brightness—features described under the UFO that are quite common in misidentifications of Venus. - The long duration of the observation (2 hours according to T1) is characteristic of an astronomical misinterpretation, and the disappearance of the UFO for half an hour after sunrise is characteristic of Venus. - Venus was in the direction indicated by the witnesses and would have been in the vicinity of the UFO if the latter were not Venus, whereas the witnesses reported a clear, starry sky and did not mention the brightest star near the UFO. The witnesses noted a movement of the UFO, which seems inconsistent with Venus: - it should be noted that the witnesses were in a car at the beginning of the observation, which could have caused an illusion of movement of the UFO in the surrounding environment and near horizon, whereas it was this environment that was changing in front of Venus due to the hilly and winding profile of the track taken by the witnesses. - T2's description could suggest a movement of the UFO occurring after the vehicle stopped (e.g., he stopped the vehicle. It was then that the beam of light disappeared, the sphere stabilized, and then moved towards the Ouipoin Koinde mountain). This description supports the previous explanation because the vehicle's stopping is followed by the sphere stabilizing. The description of its final movement towards the mountain is also consistent with this hypothesis. Indeed, a decrease in the intensity of Venus (variation in atmospheric haze) is logically interpreted by the witness as an increase in the distance of the UFO along the line of sight, which corresponds to the direction of the mountain in question. T2 reports that the beam of light disappeared after T1 activated his high beams. This conjunction is not reported by T1, who only notes that at a certain point the trapezoidal shape disappeared and I only perceived the glow of the balloon, even though it is T1 who is supposedly looking for a reaction from the UFO by activating a navigation light. The beam's interruption results from a change in the atmospheric haze, while T2's memorization and/or interpretation of a conjunction or causal link with the navigation light is attributable to the strangeness experienced, perhaps even heightened in retrospect. Regarding the observations of T3 and T4: the description of a slowly moving luminous sphere could suggest the observation of an aircraft or a satellite. However, nothing appears in the record of air operations made immediately after the observation, nor in the record of satellite passes that can be made 35 years later. The sighting is therefore strange. However, the consistency is weak. - In terms of information, we have no indication of the duration or angular size of the UFO. - We can doubt its reliability: both witnesses, T3 and T4, give a minimal account without any description of the strangeness they experienced, as if it were simply a matter of answering the questions of the police officers who approached them following reports of sightings they might have made in the neighborhood. T2 did indeed report to the police an observation recounted by T3. The short accounts of T3 and T4 are almost identical, with the same expressions and words, as if there had been some coordination before being interviewed by the police. T3 reportedly informed T2 of two previous observations similar to T2's, but did not mention the second (March 3 at 4:00 AM) to the police and provided a description of the first (March 2 at 7:00 PM) which bore little resemblance to T2's observation (very distinct direction and movements). The consistency of the observations by T3 and T4 does not appear sufficient to support their unusual nature and classify them as unexplained. Consequently: Case FOA (LA) (988) 05.03.1984: the observation by T1 and T2 is classified as A, observation of the planet Venus. Case FOA (LA) (988) 02.03.1984: the observation by T3 and T4 is classified as C, potentially unusual but unusable due to a lack of reliable information. Case FOA (LA) (988) --.03.1984: the observation of T5 is classified C, potentially not very strange but not usable due to lack of reliable information.

summary: A luminous phenomenon in the sky.
description: On February 21, 1984, at approximately 7:15 a.m., a witness in a car spotted three bright red lights in the sky. Getting out of his car, he observed for about a minute a triangle formed by the three red lights; a green light shone in the center of this triangle. The stationary phenomenon was located at an altitude of approximately 200 meters. It disappeared as it slowly moved away. No further information was gathered about this phenomenon.

summary: A cigar-shaped craft falling from the sky.
description: On February 12, 1984, a driver and his passenger saw a cylindrical shape emitting a shimmering light for three seconds. This object, which witnesses described as resembling a javelin, crossed the sky at very high speed and disappeared from sight before reaching the horizon. No further information was gathered about this phenomenon, which, based on witness descriptions, resembled an atmospheric reentry.

summary: Probable observation of atmospheric reentry
description: Around 5:00 AM on February 5, 1984, several people saw a rectangular object in the pitch-black night sky. It emitted an intense, bright blue glow, allowing them to see as clearly as in broad daylight. This object moved silently from north to south at very high speed. The observation lasted between 5 and 8 seconds; the phenomenon then disappeared over the horizon. The witnesses' descriptions suggest that this was likely an atmospheric reentry.

summary: A red ball suddenly appeared in front of a motorist.
description: After a night shift, a driver saw a red ball appear above his car. A beam of light forced him to swerve off the main road. The witness got out of his vehicle and walked toward the red ball until it disappeared. Terrified, he went to a farmer in the field bordering the road. The farmer hadn't seen the phenomenon but later stated during the investigation that, from the spot where the sighting occurred, the rising sun could be seen as a red ball. The investigation concluded that several factors, such as fatigue and glare from the rising sun, caused the optical illusion, the fear, and the driver's sudden change of direction.

summary: Nighttime observations from a vehicle of a first phenomenon (UAP 1) appearing to follow witnesses over a long distance: lack of information.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, originally classified as A, B, C, or D, which are now being re-examined to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This case, previously classified as D and named GRAND GALLARGUES (30) 1984, is part of a group of cases recently re-examined. On January 5, 1984, at approximately 2:30 a.m., two witnesses were traveling in an ambulance on the A9 motorway towards Montpellier (34). Witnesses noticed a UFO following them along the highway for about twenty kilometers. A second UFO was observed only by the second witness, who was very frightened. No unusual noises were heard during the observations. It is necessary to distinguish between two phenomena: UFO 1 and UFO 2 (see the investigation report). The physical characteristics and behavior of UFO 1 observed by the two witnesses do not correspond to any known phenomenon. However, upon further examination of the testimonies, it becomes clear that virtually all the elements of the testimonies, in addition to the drawings, diverge regarding the appearance and behavior of UFO 1, and that their quantitative and qualitative weakness prevents further verification and cross-checking that could either explain, confirm, or refute the strange and inexplicable nature of the phenomenon. This lack of consistency prevents maintaining the case in its initial classification D. Consequently, GEIPAN classifies UFO 1 as C: lack of reliable information. Regarding UAP 2 observed only by T2 (see case [A9] from Nîmes (30) towards Montpellier (34) 05/01/1984 T2), this is an astronomical misinterpretation involving the star Aldebaran, observed in a temporarily favorable geographical configuration. Part of the strangeness experienced by T2 stems from the illusion of a tracking sphere, created by the witness's own movement: the distant UAP (here, the star) gives the impression of following the witness's movement relative to the road, whereas it is the road that is moving relative to the star's fixed direction. Consequently, GEIPAN classifies UAP 2 as A: an observation of Aldebaran.
